extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / graduate students and researchers in projective/modern geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, theorems, and computational procedures concerning poles and polars relative to surfaces of the second degree (quadratic surfaces) and related projective properties (reciprocal lines, diameters, involution, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Polar plane of a point for a general second-degree surface
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the general second-degree surface (general quadratic in x,y,z), the polar plane of a given point (x0,y0,z0) is given by the bilinear form obtained by eliminating the arbitrary parameters (the coefficients) between the surface equation and the expression for a plane; explicit forms are displayed (equations (11) and (12)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The polar plane is obtained by treating the surface and the plane equation identically and equating coefficients of like powers; the text gives the explicit polynomial expression (see equations (11) and (12)) and shows how to substitute the coordinates of the given point to get the polar plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polar plane for special diagonal quadratic surface
rubrics_metrics.description: For the special surface az^2 + by^2 + cx^2 + 2a = 0 (a simpler form), the polar plane of point (x0,y0,z0) has a simpler explicit expression (equation (14)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the simplified coefficients in the general formula to produce the simpler polar-plane equation (given in the text as (14)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinates of the pole
rubrics_metrics.description: The coordinates (x0,y0,z0) of the pole of a given polar plane are found by equating the polar-plane expression (in variables) to the given plane and matching coefficients of powers of the variables, thereby solving linear relations for the pole's coordinates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the polar plane equation and the given plane as identical and equate coefficients term-by-term to solve for the pole coordinates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poles of planes through a common point lie in polar plane (duality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poles of three or more planes which pass through the same point lie in one plane, namely the polar plane of that point; conversely, the polar planes of three or more points which lie in one plane pass through the same point (the pole of that plane).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text demonstrates this by writing plane equations (15–17), substituting the common point coordinates, and showing those pole coordinates satisfy the polar equation (18). This is the fundamental duality linking concurrency of planes to collinearity/planarity of poles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion duality: plane turning about point ↔ pole moving on polar plane
rubrics_metrics.description: If a plane turns about a point in itself, its pole moves upon a plane (the polar plane of that point); conversely, if a point moves upon a plane, its polar plane turns about a point (the pole of that plane).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a kinematic description of the dual relation between points and planes in the polar correspondence; use the relation proven in article 3 to reason about loci under motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal straight lines (definition and characterization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition: Two straight lines are reciprocal when they are related as 'line of intersections of planes ↔ line joining poles of those planes' (i.e., a line formed by intersection of two planes is reciprocal to the line through the poles of those two planes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterization: If a plane turns about a fixed straight line, its pole moves in a straight line; conversely, if a point moves on a straight line, its polar turns about a fixed straight line. Use the polars of two fixed points in the fixed line to determine the straight line locus of the pole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal straight lines for families: intersection ↔ coplanarity
rubrics_metrics.description: If three or more straight lines intersect in a point, their reciprocal straight lines lie in a plane; conversely, if three or more straight lines lie in a plane, their reciprocal straight lines pass through the same point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply article 5 construction: consider families of planes through pairs of points and use the polar correspondence to show the reciprocal lines are coplanar or concurrent as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equation of reciprocity between two polar lines
rubrics_metrics.description: To find the reciprocal of a given line given by parametric linear relations y = a z + b, x = a' z + b', compute the polars of two arbitrary points on the given line, substitute into the polar equation (14), eliminate the parameter z to obtain two plane equations (equations (19)) whose intersection is the reciprocal line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: pick a generic point on the line, compute its polar, treat the point-parameter as variable and eliminate to get two plane equations; their intersection is the reciprocal. The text gives the explicit algebraic elimination steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polar of a line moving parallel to a given line is in a fixed plane
rubrics_metrics.description: If a line moves parallel to a given line (i.e., its direction coefficients fixed, intercepts variable), then its polar is always situated in a given plane; corollary: the polar of the line generating a cylindrical surface is in the same plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set the slope coefficients constant and allow intercepts to vary in the parametric line equations (article 7); substituting into the polar-formula yields one fixed plane among the two whose intersection gives the reciprocal, so the intersection line (the polar) stays in a fixed plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diameters: poles of planes parallel to a plane lie on a straight line
rubrics_metrics.description: All poles of planes that are parallel to a given plane lie in the same straight line; this straight line is called the diameter of the system conjugate to that plane. The diameter and the given plane are conjugate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive by representing the family of parallel planes with one constant pair of coefficients and variable parameter p (equation (20)), set equal to the general polar form, and show the pole coordinates satisfy two linear equations (21,22) which represent a straight line (the diameter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Centre and diametral plane; types of diameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Diameters in a system either pass through the same point (the centre), are mutually parallel, or pass through several indeterminate points. The point through which diameters pass is the centre; the plane containing the centre is the diametral plane. Conditions for finiteness or indeterminacy of the centre are given via a common denominator expression (abe − ad' − be − cf* + 2def etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the diameter equations (21,22), letting parameters vary gives three simultaneous equations whose solution yields the centre coordinates unless the common denominator vanishes, in which case the centre is at infinity or indeterminate; use the algebraic expression provided to test cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangent plane equals polar plane (tangent as polar)
rubrics_metrics.description: The tangent plane at any point (x0,y0,z0) of a surface of the second degree can be regarded as the polar of that point, and conversely that point is the pole of the tangent plane. Explicit tangent-plane equations are given (equations (24) and (26)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute tangent plane via differentiation-form or by substituting conditions for diameter conjugacy; the text demonstrates equivalence to the polar-plane equation, and gives explicit algebraic manipulations to reach the tangent-plane formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polar of a point outside the surface: plane of contact of tangent planes
rubrics_metrics.description: The polar (with respect to the quadric) of a point not on the surface is the plane of contact of the three or more tangent planes drawn from that point to the surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use article 11: tangent planes drawn from the point are polars of their respective contact points; by article 3 those contact points lie in a single plane — the polar of the external point. Corollaries about loci of contact points follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocity of contact lines and intersection of tangent planes
rubrics_metrics.description: The line joining the points of contact of two tangent planes to a quadric and the line of intersection of those two tangent planes are reciprocal straight lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows immediately from article 4: intersection line is reciprocal to line joining poles, and in this case poles are points of contact (article 10 corollary). Use this to deduce dual relations between chords and intersection lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocals of straight lines in a plane are chords through same point
rubrics_metrics.description: The reciprocals of three or more straight lines situated in the same plane (and not meeting the quadric) are chords of the surface passing through the same point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine articles 5 and 12: reciprocals of coplanar lines are concurrent chords (they meet in a single point), giving relationships between planar line-systems and chord systems on the quadric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duality of inscribed and circumscribed polyhedra on a quadric
rubrics_metrics.description: If a polyhedron is inscribed in a quadric and a circumscribed polyhedron drawn through corresponding tangent planes at the vertices, then the faces of one polyhedron are the polars of the angular points (vertices) of the other; intersecting lines correspond to reciprocal lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an application of articles 10–12: faces ↔ vertex polars, and intersection-line reciprocity follows from previous reciprocity theorems. Use this theorem to construct dual polyhedra relative to a given quadric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefinite number of quadrics through eight points; diameters' concurrency properties
rubrics_metrics.description: An indefinite number of second-order surfaces may pass through eight given points in space; when sections are cut parallel to a given plane, the diameters conjugate to these sections either all meet in the same point or pass through several indeterminate points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: general quadratic has nine coefficients; eight point conditions leave one free coefficient, giving a family of quadrics. The diameter equations then have one indeterminate coefficient, producing the concurrency or indeterminacy behaviors described (see article 15).

rubrics_metrics.name: Planes of contact of tangents from a fixed point to the family of quadrics through eight points intersect in a fixed line
rubrics_metrics.description: If from a given point tangent planes are drawn to all quadrics passing through eight fixed points, the planes of contact intersect in one and the same straight line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived in article 16 by considering the family with one indeterminate coefficient and showing the contact-plane equations reduce to a fixed line in the appropriate plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planes of contact for a fixed point across quadrics through seven points concur
rubrics_metrics.description: For quadrics passing through seven given points, the planes of contact drawn from a fixed point intersect in the same point (i.e., the planes of contact all pass through a common point).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since two coefficients remain indeterminate when seven points are specified, the resulting contact-plane equations possess a common intersection point (article 17).

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms and equations of involution (six-segment formulations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The equation of an involution by means of six segments may be expressed in twelve (or more) equivalent algebraic forms; the text displays canonical arrangements and shows how permutations and circulations produce the family of equivalent expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fundamental equation and its derived circulations are given explicitly; use symmetry and permutation arguments to obtain the full set of equivalent involution equations (see XI–XII).

rubrics_metrics.name: Involution of eight points: anharmonic ratios equality
rubrics_metrics.description: In an involution of eight points, the anharmonic ratio of any four of them equals the anharmonic ratio of the remaining four (derivation provided by combining Apollonian properties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the presented equalities (compositions of ratios) to show the required equalities of anharmonic ratios (see XIII).

rubrics_metrics.name: Special cases of involution: centre, infinite and double points
rubrics_metrics.description: If one point of a conjugate pair coincides with the centre of involution, its mate is infinitely distant, and conversely; when a pair coalesces to a point, that point is a double point (focus) of the involution. The seven equations of involution reduce under these hypotheses (corollaries given).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the relations ao·oa' = co·oc' etc.; examine limiting/coalescing cases and use the reduced equations provided to classify double points and infinite points (see XIV and corollaries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection between systems of circles with a common radical axis and involution
rubrics_metrics.description: If a family of circles share the same radical axis, the intersections of those circles with the line joining their centres are divided in involution; moreover, any transversal through the radical centre cuts the circles in points that are in involution with that centre as the involution centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct circles with diameters at conjugate segment pairs; use the radical-axis property ao·oa' = bo·ob' etc. to infer involution of intersection points and properties of double points in tangency cases (see scholium to XIV).

rubrics_metrics.name: System of involution-radiants: sine relations among angles
rubrics_metrics.description: If segments from the points of an involution to any point S are denoted by rays, then the same involution relations hold for the sines of the angles formed by these rays as held for the segments themselves (sine form of involution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace linear segments by sine-of-angle terms according to relations in (XV.1); the same algebraic structure yields involution relations for angular systems (useful for spherical and angular versions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection preserves involution (line and plane projections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every projection of an involution system by linear radiants onto another line in the same plane (or by planes meeting in a line) results in an involution system on the image line; similarly for projections onto the sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use properties (XV.4–6): projective maps by linear radiants or by planes meeting in a line preserve anharmonic ratios and hence preserve involution structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desargues/Quadrilateral property on circle/conic: anharmonic equality
rubrics_metrics.description: For a quadrilateral PQRS inscribed in a circle and any transversal GH cutting the circle, the anharmonic ratios of angles at opposite vertices P and R are equal; consequently the transversal is divided at its intersections with the quadrilateral and circle in involution (Pappus criterion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove by expressing sines of arcs and using symmetry; then generalize by projection to any conic (xv.1–3). This yields the classical Desargues property linking inscribed quadrilaterals and involution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involution produced by multiple conics circumscribed about same quadrilateral
rubrics_metrics.description: If two or more conics are circumscribed about the same quadrilateral, then for any transversal the collection of intersection points with those conics (and with opposite sides/diagonals) forms an involution; with many conics this produces involutions of many points (e.g., 2n points).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the fact that four common points AA'BB' determine a common centre O of involution; equalities of products AO·OA' = BO·OB' etc. extend across the family of conics (see XVIII).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anharmonic ratios of tangent intersections are preserved
rubrics_metrics.description: If SP and SP' are two tangents to a circle and are cut by four other tangents in corresponding points, then the two systems of intersection points on SP and SP' have equal anharmonic ratios; the statement extends to tangents of any conic by projection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove using central angles to the circle's center and angle-equality arguments (xx.1–3), then project to conics to obtain the general tangent statement (xxi).
